This paper presents the empirical demand-side case for inflation immunity as the largest unmet financial need in modern history. Drawing on longitudinal survey data from Ipsos (30 countries, approximately 20,000 respondents per month, over a decade of continuous measurement), the Gallup World Poll (107 countries), the European Central Bank's Consumer Expectations Survey (19,000 adult consumers across 11 eurozone countries), the Ipsos Cost of Living Monitor, the Economic Policy Institute, the U.S. Federal Reserve, the U.S. Census Bureau, and Opportunity Insights at Harvard University, it establishes three convergent findings. First, inflation was the number one global concern for 33 of 34 consecutive months in the most comprehensive longitudinal survey of public priorities ever conducted, and economic anxiety dominates public concern across 107 countries by a margin of more than two-to-one over any other category. Second, the erosion of purchasing power is a structural condition spanning five decades: since 1979, US productivity has grown 2.7 times faster than typical worker compensation, the probability that a child will out-earn their parents has declined from approximately 90 percent to approximately 50 percent, and housing has shifted from roughly two times median annual income to more than five times. Third, forward-looking anxiety is intensifying: 68 percent of respondents across 30 countries expect inflation to rise further, and perceived inflation consistently exceeds measured inflation by 50 to 60 percent. Together, these findings demonstrate that the demand for deterministic purchasing power preservation is not theoretical or speculative but the most widely shared and most empirically documented economic anxiety on earth. The paper concludes that no existing financial product provides deterministic, real-time inflation immunity, identifying a structural gap between universal demand and absent supply. GENO Research Series, Paper XVII. Originally published on the Geno Project website (geno.ac).

sections.heading: The response of low-income households to the cost-of-living crisis in
paragraphs: The Ipsos Cost of Living Monitor, a comprehensive study, delves into the response of low-income households to the escalating cost-of-living crisis in Ireland. This crisis, exacerbated by rising inflation, has significantly impacted the financial stability of these households, leading to a notable increase in material deprivation. The study, conducted between May and June 2024, examines how these households have adapted to the economic pressures and the challenges they encountered in accessing government benefits and support services during the cost-of-living crisis. [[S6|OpenAlex research index]]

The research employed a cross-sectional survey method, leveraging techniques from behavioral science to enhance recall and minimize biases in responses. The study involved a nationally representative sample of 1,615 financial decision-makers from low-income households, recruited from online market research panels and in-person in low-income areas. Participants reported on changes in their day-to-day spending, borrowing, and saving due to the cost-of-living crisis, focusing on the period following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. [[S6|OpenAlex research index]]

The study found that most low-income households responded to the economic pressures by adjusting their spending habits and borrowing. They also reported using government benefits and support services, but encountered significant administrative burdens, which became barriers to accessing these supports. The study highlights the importance of tailored support and adaptability in addressing the challenges faced by low-income households during the cost-of-living crisis. [[S6|OpenAlex research index]]

The research also draws on the ECAIL trial, a mixed-methods implementation study that evaluated a multicomponent intervention for childhood obesity prevention among hard-to-reach families. The study compared eligibility and participation before and after the resumption of the intervention following the suspension due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The findings indicate that eligibility increased from 29.7% (n = 955) pre-pandemic to 33.6% (n = 849) after resumption, while the distribution of vulnerability criteria remained similar across periods. The qualitative findings suggest that dietitians' satisfaction and participants' enthusiasm for the resumption of home visits, particularly in addressing social isolation, were positively received. [[S6|OpenAlex research index]]

The study also found that the introduction of a pre-visit COVID-19 questionnaire was associated with fewer failed home visits after resumption. The integration of quantitative and qualitative findings indicated sustained and in some cases strengthened provider engagement despite the strain on hospital services due to the pandemic. The rapid resumption of home-based services emerged as a promising implementation strategy, suggesting that a complex intervention can maintain reach and acceptability through adaptive implementation under major contextual disruptions. [[S6|OpenAlex research index]]

The research underscores the importance of tailored support and adaptability in addressing the challenges faced by low-income households during the cost-of-living crisis. The findings highlight the need for continuous support and adaptation to ensure that these households can navigate the economic pressures effectively. [[S6|OpenAlex research index]]

sections.heading: Examining changes in the prevalence of cost‐motivated alcohol reduction attempts
paragraphs: ### Section 8: Examining Changes in the Prevalence of Cost-Motivated Alcohol Reduction Attempts [[S1|Addiction]] In the context of a cost-of-living crisis and alcohol duty reforms, a population survey of risky drinkers in Great Britain revealed significant changes in the prevalence of cost-motivated alcohol reduction attempts. The study, conducted between January 2021 and December 2024, aimed to estimate the monthly prevalence of cost-motivated alcohol reduction attempts among risky drinkers. [[S1|Addiction]] Overall, 1355 participants reported making a cost-motivated alcohol reduction attempt. This represents a monthly weighted prevalence of 7.0% in December 2024, up from 4.6% in January 2021.

The prevalence ratio (PR) indicates that the prevalence of cost-motivated alcohol reduction attempts increased by 54% over the period, equating to approximately 1.1 million people attempting to reduce their drinking among risky drinkers in 2024. [[S1|Addiction]] The pattern of results was similar when the outcome was restricted to alcohol reduction attempts only motivated by cost. The proportion of all cost-motivated alcohol reduction attempts increased from 12.4% to 19.7% (PR = 1.58, 95% CI = 1.39-1.77), rather than an overall increase in the prevalence of alcohol reduction attempts, which remained relatively stable at an average of 36.0%. [[S1|Addiction]] The findings suggest that during a period of increasing financial pressures in Great Britain, alcohol reduction attempts were increasingly motivated by cost.

However, the overall prevalence of reduction attempts did not increase. This indicates that while the prevalence of cost-motivated alcohol reduction attempts increased, the overall prevalence of alcohol reduction attempts remained stable. [[S1|Addiction]] The study highlights the complex interplay between economic pressures and alcohol consumption, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions to address both the affordability of alcohol and the reduction of alcohol consumption.
